content: The Moro reflex, also referred to as the startle reflex, is one of the primitive reflexes observed in infants. It can be seen in an incomplete form in premature infants after the 28th week of gestation and typically becomes fully developed by the 34th week of gestation, during the third trimester. This reflex is normally present in all newborns and infants up to the age of 4 or 5 months. The absence of the Moro reflex is indicative of a significant motor system disorder. If the Moro reflex is absent or inadequate on one side of the body, it may suggest conditions such as hemiplegia, brachial plexus palsy, or a fractured clavicle. Persistence of the Moro reflex beyond 4 or 5 months of age is generally associated with severe neurological abnormalities. This reflex was first identified and described by Austrian pediatrician Ernst Moro (1874–1951). The Moro reflex is triggered by unexpected loud noises or a sensation of falling. It is considered the only innate fear response in human newborns. The famous Little Albert experiment utilized the startle reflex in classical conditioning to induce a fear of white, fuzzy objects. The Moro reflex is significant in assessing the integration of the central nervous system (CNS). It consists of four distinct components: the startle response, abduction (spreading out of the arms), adduction (bringing the arms back in), and usually crying. The absence of any component (except crying) or asymmetry in the movements is considered abnormal. Similarly, persistence of the reflex in older infants, children, or adults is also abnormal. However, in individuals with cerebral palsy, persistence and exaggeration of the Moro reflex are commonly observed. In adults, the startle reflex is modulated by the expressions and reactions of observers.
